rules.surface_condition: positions where the token immediately AFTER the marker is a present-participial / -ing verb that commonly introduces a clause continuation (e.g. causing, facing, resulting, leading, following)
rules.blamed_rule: - A marker that falls where a comma or parenthetical comma surrounds a self-contained adjunct (e.g., "yesterday,", "on Tuesday,", "as sources said,") often yields high scores if both sides can be translated faithfully by themselves. (Prediction to test: cuts after a comma that closes an embedded adjunct can score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: In [Scoring Rules] add a targeted downward override: if the token immediately after the marker is one of {causing, facing, resulting, leading, following, resulting} then reduce the predicted score into a low-risk band (target 10–35). Rationale: present-participial continuations frequently overturn or continue the left chunk (high contradiction / low standalone faithfulness) even when a preceding comma would otherwise encourage an uplift.

rules.surface_condition: positions immediately after concrete-place / concrete-object nouns that are often comma‑terminated adjuncts (examples seen: oahu, maldives, gauge, ship, coffin, mummy) when the token immediately AFTER the marker is a finite auxiliary or finite lexical verb (was, is, are, reached, will, be)
rules.blamed_rule: - A marker that falls where a comma or parenthetical comma surrounds a self-contained adjunct (e.g., "yesterday,", "on Tuesday,", "as sources said,") often yields high scores if both sides can be translated faithfully by themselves. (Prediction to test: cuts after a comma that closes an embedded adjunct can score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: Add a sharpening of the comma-adjunct uplift: if the token immediately BEFORE the marker is in {oahu, maldives, gauge, ship, coffin, mummy, light} AND the token immediately AFTER the marker is one of {was, is, are, reached, will, be, were}, then lower the score into a conservative band (target 5–35). Rationale: place/object adjuncts followed by finite predicates are a frequent source of contradiction / bad standalone translation despite the visual comma; the general comma uplift should not override this signal.

rules.surface_condition: positions that split a role/designation or class-word immediately before a following name/label (examples of left tokens: governor, class, former, president, minister, senator, dr, mr, ms, mrs)
rules.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: Introduce a protective lowering for title/role splits: if the token immediately BEFORE the marker is any of {governor, president, senator, minister, dr, mr, ms, mrs, former, class} then reduce the score into a cautious band (target 10–35). Rationale: splitting a designation/class token from the following name/appositive frequently yields fragments or appositional mismatches in single-side translation; the generic named-phrase uplift should be suppressed here.

tie_fix: Ties still arise when per-bucket heuristics produce identical integers after rounding and the micro-offset is too small to survive integer rounding. Increase the deterministic micro-offset used before rounding (e.g., offset = 0.01 × token_position_index) or apply a small token-class priority offset (prespecified, numeric) before rounding so that the integer rounding preserves the deterministic ordering.
summary: The prompt's comma/adjunct and named-phrase uplifts are too blunt: they let markers with right-side continuations (present-participles or finite predicates) or title/name appositions score very high despite measured contradiction or fragmenthood. Add targeted downward overrides that (1) penalize right-side present-participles, (2) disable the comma-adjunct uplift for concrete-place/object nouns followed by finite verbs, and (3) suppress named-phrase uplift when a role/class token is immediately before the cut. These rules are surface-token anchored and measurable on the given cases.
